title: Trump Rolls Back Fuel Rules: What It Means for Cars
summary: Imagine if your family's car could go farther on a gallon of gas. That's what fuel economy rules are about. Under President Biden, the rules said cars and light trucks should average about 50.4 miles per gallon by 2031. That's like driving from New York City to Philadelphia on one gallon of gas! But on Saturday, President Donald Trump announced he is rolling back those rules. He called Biden's plan an "EV mandate" — even though there is no law that says you must buy an electric car. Trump said the new standards will "take the waste out of building cars in America" and mean "LOWER PRICES" for families. In December 2025, he proposed a new target of about 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031 — more than 30 percent lower than Biden's rule. The rules are called CAFE standards, and they've been around since 1975. They work by making carmakers balance gas guzzlers with efficient cars. Trump didn't give exact numbers this time, but his Transportation Secretary said an announcement is "COMING MONDAY." Supporters say this helps car companies and buyers. Critics worry it will increase pollution and make the U.S. fall behind other countries in electric cars.
why_it_matters: Car rules decide how much your family spends on gas and how clean the air is where you live, so this argument is really about the cars you will ride in for years.

Cars and trucks that burn a lot of gasoline.

What did the Transportation Secretary say about the new rules?

background_read: CAFE standards are U.S. rules that began in 1975, after an oil crisis in the 1970s made gasoline suddenly expensive and hard to find.
President Biden (the U.S. president from 2021 to 2025) wanted cars to use less gas and pushed for more electric cars.
The Transportation Secretary is the person in charge of the U.S. Department of Transportation, the government office that helps decide car rules.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump, President Biden, and the Transportation Secretary.
WHAT: Trump announced he is rolling back Biden-era fuel economy rules and proposed a much lower target of about 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031.
WHERE: The United States — the rules apply to new cars and light trucks sold all across the country.
WHY: These rules change how much gas cars use, how much families pay at the pump, and how much pollution cars put into the air.

perspectives.description: They say lighter rules let car companies build cars more cheaply, which can mean lower prices for families and fewer government demands on businesses.
They worry that weaker rules will mean more pollution, more gasoline burned, and the U.S. falling behind other countries that are making electric cars.
Fuel rules have changed many times since 1975, and this debate is really about balancing three things: what cars cost, how much they pollute, and what kinds of cars companies choose to build.
